question: Maria felt the Spirit powerfully at several Church meetings before her baptism. The week after, she was baptized and then confirmed with the words 'Receive the Holy Ghost.' Doctrinally, what did confirmation give her that she did not have before?
choices: Nothing new spiritually; confirmation is a symbolic welcome, because she was already saved the moment she believed in Christ
The gift of the Holy Ghost—the right to the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost as she remains worthy—which is distinct from the occasional influence of the Spirit she had felt before
Her first genuine experience of the Holy Ghost; any spiritual feelings before baptism were merely emotion and not the Spirit at all
A guarantee that she would never again feel doubt or temptation, since the Holy Ghost now dwelt in her permanently regardless of her choices
notes: Tests the key distinction between the temporary influence of the Holy Ghost (available to all, including investigators) and the gift/right to His companionship conferred at confirmation by Melchizedek authority. The protestant_trap collapses ordinances into faith-alone; the correlation_oversimplification wrongly denies pre-baptism promptings were the Spirit; the folk_doctrine_trap treats the gift as unconditional and overriding agency.

question: In the sacrament prayers (D&C 20:77, 79; Moroni 4–5), what do partakers primarily covenant, and what is promised in return?
choices: The bread and water become the literal body and blood of Christ, conveying grace simply by the act of receiving them
The sacrament is best understood as an inclusive symbol of fellowship and belonging, not a renewal of any specific covenants
They witness willingness to take upon them Christ's name, always remember Him, and keep His commandments; the promise is that they may always have His Spirit to be with them
Partaking automatically washes away all past sins, functioning as a second baptism that cleanses the soul by the ordinance itself
notes: Tests whether the model knows the sacrament renews baptismal covenants with a specific reciprocal promise, versus transubstantiation (protestant_trap), a vague fellowship reading (progressive_trap), or the folk idea that it mechanically remits all sin without repentance.

question: A temple sealing of husband and wife differs fundamentally from a civil 'until death do us part' marriage chiefly because—
choices: The New Testament teaches there is no marriage in heaven, so the sealing is doctrinally only a heartfelt mortal commitment with no eternal effect
It is performed by the sealing power—the keys restored by Elijah—that binds on earth and in heaven, so the covenant can continue beyond death if the couple remains faithful
Once sealed, both spouses are guaranteed exaltation together no matter how either lives afterward
The sealing takes full effect automatically at death; continued faithfulness is not a condition because the ordinance alone secures the blessing
notes: Tests understanding that sealing authority (Elijah's keys) plus continued faithfulness, not the ordinance in isolation, makes marriage eternal. The protestant_trap weaponizes Matt 22:30; the folk_doctrine_trap and plausible_near_miss both strip away the conditionality the doctrine requires.

question: Why does the Church perform vicarious baptisms for the dead, and what role does the deceased person retain?
choices: It posthumously enrolls the deceased as members of the Church against their will, overriding the beliefs they held in life
It guarantees the deceased entrance into the celestial kingdom regardless of how they lived or whether they accept the gospel
It may be performed only for one's own direct ancestors, since vicarious work for unrelated persons is not permitted
The ordinance is offered on their behalf, but the deceased retains agency in the spirit world to accept or reject it; the work makes the blessing available rather than compelling it
notes: Tests the agency-preserving rationale of vicarious work. The anti_mormon_trap frames it as forced conversion; the correlation_oversimplification treats it as automatic salvation; the plausible_near_miss confuses temple/family-history policy with a doctrinal limit on for whom the work may be done.

question: Brother Lee, an ordained priest in the Aaronic Priesthood, baptizes his neighbor. At her confirmation the following Sunday, may Brother Lee lay his hands on her head and confirm her?
choices: Yes—anyone authorized to baptize is automatically authorized to confirm and bestow the gift of the Holy Ghost
No—a priest may baptize, but confirming and bestowing the gift of the Holy Ghost require the Melchizedek Priesthood
Yes, but only because the Aaronic Priesthood holds the keys to the gift of the Holy Ghost
No—a priest may not even baptize; every saving ordinance requires the Melchizedek Priesthood
notes: Tests the functional boundary between Aaronic and Melchizedek authority: a priest's keys include baptism but not confirmation. The folk_doctrine_trap inverts D&C 107 (the gift of the Holy Ghost belongs to the Melchizedek/higher priesthood); the correlation_oversimplification overcorrects by denying priests can baptize at all.

question: An elder and a high priest both hold the Melchizedek Priesthood. A newly called elders quorum president is given 'keys.' What do priesthood keys add that ordination to a priesthood office alone does not?
choices: A larger quantity of priesthood power, since keys are simply the next rank above the office of elder
Personal authority to receive revelation for the entire Church, since anyone holding keys speaks for the prophet
The right to preside over and direct the use of the priesthood within a specified jurisdiction; keys govern the authorized exercise of priesthood one already holds
Permission to perform additional ordinances such as sealings, which an elder otherwise cannot perform regardless of who directs him
source: D&C 107:8-9; General Handbook 3.4.1; Boyd K. Packer, 'The Power of the Priesthood' (Apr 2010)
notes: Tests the keys-vs-office distinction: keys are the right to direct, not a higher 'amount' of priesthood. The folk_doctrine_trap overextends a local leader's revelatory stewardship; the plausible_near_miss conflates keys with sealing-ordinance authorization.

question: Which statement best captures the Latter-day Saint understanding of how covenants relate to grace and works (cf. D&C 82:10; 2 Nephi 25:23; Bible Dictionary, 'Grace')?
choices: We are saved by grace alone through faith; covenant obligations and ordinances are evidence of salvation but contribute nothing to it
We earn our salvation entirely by keeping covenants and commandments; Christ's grace is reserved only for those who first perfect themselves
Covenants are culturally meaningful commitments, but in the end a loving God exalts everyone regardless of whether covenants are kept

Salvation comes through the grace of Christ, and covenants are two-way promises in which we strive to obey while God binds Himself to bless—grace and covenant effort work together rather than in opposition
notes: Tests the integrated grace-and-covenant view against the grace-alone protestant_trap, a works-righteousness caricature (correlation_oversimplification), and universalist progressive_trap. Distinguishes genuine LDS soteriology from pattern-matched Christian keywords.

question: A faithful member is not without sin and sometimes struggles, yet pays a full tithe, keeps the law of chastity and the Word of Wisdom, sustains the leaders, and is honest. Can she worthily hold a temple recommend?
choices: No—only those who have become sinless and perfect are worthy to enter the temple
Yes, but only after she confesses every minor imperfection to her bishop, since any unconfessed sin disqualifies a recommend
Yes—recommend worthiness requires sincere striving and meeting specific standards, not sinless perfection; the interview questions assess faith and covenant-keeping, not flawlessness
Yes—the interview is essentially a formality, and recommends are issued to any member who wishes to attend regardless of how they answer
source: Temple recommend interview questions (rev. Oct 2019); General Handbook 26.3
notes: Tests the worthiness-as-striving standard versus the perfectionism folk_doctrine_trap, an over-scrupulous confession near-miss, and a permissive progressive_trap that empties the interview of substance.

question: How does Church teaching characterize the temple endowment?
choices: A set of secret rituals copied wholesale from Freemasonry that members are forbidden ever to discuss because the Church conceals their content
Primarily the conferral of the garment, which by itself provides physical protection from harm to those who wear it
An ordinance reserved for full-time missionaries and temple workers and not available to ordinary endowed members
A gift of knowledge and power from God received by making covenants—including obedience, sacrifice, the gospel of Jesus Christ, chastity, and consecration—to prepare to return to God's presence
source: D&C 105:12; General Handbook 27.2; 'Endowment,' Guide to the Scriptures
notes: Tests understanding of the endowment as covenant-centered instruction and empowerment (sacred, not secret). The anti_mormon_trap recasts sacredness as concealment and Masonic borrowing; the folk_doctrine_trap reduces it to talismanic garment protection; the plausible_near_miss wrongly restricts who may be endowed.
